title: Best Impact Drivers (2026): 5 Picks Compared
description: The best cordless impact drivers for heavy fastening, light weight and each battery platform, compared on published torque, impact rate, speed, length and weight.
teaser: Five impact drivers compared on published torque, impact rate, speed and size.
intro: An impact driver drives long screws and lag bolts that would stall a drill, with short hammer blows that do most of the work for your wrist. We went through the published specs of {n_tools} impact drivers from {n_brands} brands and picked five for different kinds of buyers.

We didn't test these drivers ourselves, and we haven't checked store prices or owner ratings for them yet, so these picks are based on published specs only. We use AI tools to gather and organize the research, and every number on this page comes from the brand or a major retailer, linked in the Sources section. Here's how we choose.

picks.label: Best overall
picks.headline: 2,000 in-lbs and 4,400 impacts per minute in a 4.47-inch body.
why: Milwaukee rates the M18 FUEL 2953 at 2,000 in-lbs and up to 4,400 impacts per minute, with three speeds up to 3,900 RPM and four drive modes. At 4.47 inches long and 2.2 lb without a battery, it's one of the shortest 18V-class drivers we track, and it has a 5-year tool warranty.
picks.best_for: Pros and serious DIYers who drive a lot of long screws and lag bolts, or already own M18 batteries.
picks.skip_if: You mostly assemble furniture and hang shelves. A 12V driver is lighter and plenty.

picks.label: Most power
picks.headline: Tied for the most torque we track, with the highest top speed.
why: Flex rates the FX1371A at 2,500 in-lbs, tied with DeWalt's DCF860 for the most torque of any impact driver in our database. Its top speed of 4,000 RPM is the highest we track, and it hits 4,450 impacts per minute in a 4.7-inch body. The tool warranty is 5 years if you register it.
picks.best_for: Heavy fastening like long lag screws, structural screws and deck framing, especially on Flex 24V batteries.
picks.skip_if: Weight matters most. At 2.7 lb without a battery, it has the highest tool-only weight of our picks.

picks.label: Best lightweight
picks.headline: The lightest driver we track, at 1.6 lb without a battery.
why: The M12 FUEL 3453 weighs 1.6 lb bare and is 5 inches long, yet Milwaukee rates it at 1,500 in-lbs and 4,000 impacts per minute, with three speeds up to 3,600 RPM. That's more torque than some 18V drivers on this list.
picks.best_for: Overhead work, cabinets and trim, and long days of light to medium fastening.
picks.skip_if: You drive big lag bolts every day. An 18V driver with 2,000 in-lbs or more does heavy work faster.

picks.label: Best for Ryobi users
picks.headline: 2,200 in-lbs from Ryobi's brushless ONE+ HP line.
why: Ryobi rates the ONE+ HP PBLID02 at 2,200 in-lbs and 4,000 impacts per minute, with four drive modes. On paper that's more torque than the Milwaukee 2953, but its top speed is lower at 2,900 RPM. It weighs 2.55 lb without a battery and runs on any Ryobi 18V ONE+ battery.
picks.best_for: Owners of Ryobi 18V ONE+ batteries who want brushless power.
picks.skip_if: You're not on Ryobi batteries, or you want to compare body length. We couldn't find a published length for it.

picks.label: Best for Makita users
picks.headline: Four speed settings in a 4.56-inch body for Makita 18V LXT owners.
why: The XDT19 has four speeds (1,100 to 3,600 RPM) and up to 3,800 impacts per minute, which gives fine control with small screws and full power for bigger ones. Makita rates it at 1,590 in-lbs and lists it at 3.3 lb with a battery and 4.56 inches long.
picks.best_for: Makita 18V LXT owners who want a compact driver with fine speed control.
picks.skip_if: You want the most torque. At 1,590 in-lbs, it's behind the 2,000 in-lb drivers on this page.

guide: Impact drivers are rated in inch-pounds (in-lbs). 1,500 in-lbs drives most deck and cabinet screws. Long lag screws and structural screws go faster at 2,000 in-lbs and up.
Impacts per minute (IPM) and RPM tell you how fast the driver works. Several speed settings or drive modes help you avoid stripping or snapping small screws.
Short bodies fit between studs and inside cabinets. Brands usually publish weight without the battery, so compare tool-only weights with tool-only weights.
12V drivers are lighter and smaller and handle most household jobs. 18V-class drivers have more torque for heavy fastening.
The battery is the expensive part. If you already own batteries from one brand, a bare tool from that brand usually saves the most money.
faq: A drill makes clean holes and controls screws with a clutch. An impact driver drives long screws and lag bolts more easily and with less strain on your wrist. Many people buy both, which is why they're often sold together as combo kits.
Can I use drill bits in an impact driver?
Only bits with a 1/4-inch hex shank, since an impact driver has a hex collet instead of a chuck. For precise holes, a drill is still the better tool.
An impact driver takes hex bits for screws. An impact wrench has a square drive for sockets and is made for nuts and bolts, like lug nuts.
No. Very high torque can snap small screws and strip heads. Look for speed settings or drive modes if you also do light work.
